checks.label: Twelve screens: five that show and seven puzzles, alternating to the ninth and ending on three mixed puzzles
Each winding of the 440 V supply has 440 ÷ 1.732 = 254 V across it
The fault current is 254 V over the loop: 508 A on TN (0.5 Ω), 2.3 A on TT (10 + 100 = 110 Ω), 2.5 mA on IT (100 kΩ) and 0.17 A through 1,500 Ω, as the readout shows them
What happens: the breaker trips on TN, the RCD on TT, and on IT and through 1,500 Ω the supply runs on with the alarm lit
Screen 6: electrodes of 20 Ω and 200 Ω make a 220 Ω loop, so 254 ÷ 220 = 1.15 A, shown as 1.2 A, and the RCD trips
The more the loop resists, the less current flows: most on TN, then TT, then High impedance, least on IT
Every lit loop is closed: it leaves the star point up L1's winding and comes back to the star point
The trip or the alarm shows within 3 s of the fault going on
Before an answer, no puzzle's picture shows its result: no fault is on, no loop is lit, and the switch is not yet where a right answer sets it
T stands for earth, from the French word terre, and I for isolated: the TN and TT drawings tie the star point to earth, and the IT drawing does not
In a TN system the first fault is interrupted by overcurrent protection, a circuit-breaker: here the breaker trips
In an IT system the source is isolated from earth while the exposed conductive parts are connected to earth: the IT drawing joins the star point to nothing and still bonds the frame to the hull
In an IT system the first fault to earth causes no disconnection, and the current that flows is measured in mA
Unearthed distribution prevents the immediate loss of an essential service from an earth fault: on IT the motor runs on
